context: The example starts with 12 elements and a root value of 9 at index 0. The new element is 7. Another 7, already at index 4, stays there throughout. The role column in each table distinguishes the two.

The tree and array show the same storage. The array stores nodes in level order, from top to bottom and left to right within each level, starting at index 0. For a non-root position i, the parent index is (i−1)/2 rounded down. The child indices are 2i+1 and 2i+2. An out-of-bounds index means that child is absent. Indices distinguish nodes with equal values.
description: First append the new element to the level-order array to preserve the complete binary tree shape. Then sift upward along the parent path. Swap only when the current value is greater than its parent. Stop as soon as it is no greater than its parent or reaches the root. In this example, the new 7 rises along indices 12 → 5 → 2 in two swaps.

Each storage table is titled by operation and step. A new table appears only when the array changes. Steps that only compare, stop, or clear highlighting refer by full title to the table with the same contents. Each step still gives the current size, root, and operation.

summary: Append the new element, then compare and swap it with successive parents to restore the max-heap.
title: Inserting an element into a max-heap
